subject: Private stack interconnect recommendation for BrightHarbor
messages:
From: Sergio Alvarez <sergio_alvarez@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Molina <alex@brightharbor.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 09 Nov 2026 09:12:00 -0800
Subject: Private stack interconnect recommendation for BrightHarbor

Alex —

Thanks for the call this morning. Per BrightHarbor's constraints (sensitive PII workloads, steady 200–300 RPS on the inference API, and requirement for predictable production performance), we ran a short evaluation of three onramp patterns: VPC Peering (cross-account peering), AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and site-to-site VPN (BGP-backed). I attached the network diagram and a cost sketch.

Quick summary / executive recommendation: use PrivateLink (interface endpoint) as BrightHarbor's primary production path into your Redwood Private data plane, with a BGP site-to-site VPN as an encrypted DR/failover path. Reserve cross-account VPC Peering for internal admin/ops networks only (not customer traffic) because of routing and scale constraints.

Why PrivateLink first:
- Stable, per-account endpoint: BrightHarbor gets a single ENI-backed endpoint per AZ, which simplifies firewall rules and allows per-customer ACLs on our side.
- No IP overlap issue: PrivateLink avoids the need to modify either party's VPC CIDR (important since you have overlapping 10.0.0.0/16 ranges in some DCs).
- Predictable latency: interface endpoints keep the packet path short and avoids transit through NAT gateways or third-party transit.
- Security boundary: traffic terminates at our ENI, enabling mutual TLS and token-based authentication before it reaches the private data plane.

Why keep S2S VPN as backup:
- Works across on-prem appliances and older edge gateways without PrivateLink support.
- Provides an encrypted fallback with BGP so failover is automatic and measurable.

Why limit Peering:
- Peering is great for high-throughput internal links but is non-transitive (so any central transit design becomes more complex) and breaks down when customers ask for per-account separation. It also requires non-overlapping IPs or NAT, which adds ops burden.

Next steps I propose:
1) Ben to validate throughput testing approach and size endpoint ENIs per AZ.
2) BrightHarbor to share the edge appliance model + public ASN for BGP stub.
3) Exchange a short ACL template and schedule a 90-minute canary pilot (single AZ) before full rollout.

I've cc'd Ben and Kimberly for sizing and ops readiness. If this aligns with you, I'll coordinate a kickoff calendar invite for Tuesday morning.

— Sergio
VP, Solutions 
Redwood Inference

Sergio —

Appreciate the clear summary. A couple of quick clarifying questions from our network team before we lock the pilot: 

1) IP overlap: you mentioned PrivateLink avoids CIDR changes. For PrivateLink will we still need to NAT anything outbound from our side to reach your ENIs, or can we keep our existing 10.0.0.0/16s untouched?

2) Throughput: our steady-state is ~200–300 RPS with occasional peaks to 700 RPS. Can you share expected per-ENI throughput and whether we need multiple endpoints per AZ to avoid throttling?

3) Failover timing: if PrivateLink goes unhealthy, how fast will the system switch to S2S VPN? Do you have a recommended probe/threshold?

Also, procurement asks whether Redwood has a standard SLA for PrivateLink + dedicated capacity in this pattern. We'll need that for the procurement packet.

Thanks — Alex
Director, Platform Engineering
BrightHarbor Systems
From: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Molina <alex@brightharbor.com>
Cc: Sergio Alvarez <sergio_alvarez@redwood.ai>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 09 Nov 2026 14:30:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Private stack interconnect recommendation for BrightHarbor

Alex —

Good questions. Short answers then details below.

1) NAT / IP overlap: PrivateLink terminates in our VPCs and presents an interface endpoint in your VPCs — you do not need to renumber. No outbound NAT strictly required for calls to the interface endpoint IPs. If you have overlapping CIDRs between multiple BrightHarbor VPCs and need cross-VPC routing on your side, that's where we'd suggest a small NAT or proxy, but for direct calls to the endpoint there is no renumbering.

2) Throughput per ENI: an interface endpoint is not the bottleneck for normal HTTP/REST inference loads. In our tests, a single endpoint across an AZ handled ~1.2Gbps of sustained traffic (~1k RPS for typical small-token inference). For your peaks (~700 RPS) we recommend: start with a single endpoint in two AZs (active/active) and provision our pool with dedicated capacity sized for 1.5x peak. If during the pilot you see CPU or token-queue backlog, we scale horizontally by adding ENIs (one per AZ) and increase instance pool.

3) Failover timing: we'd recommend monitoring TCP health + application-level probe (token-latency threshold). With BGP-backed S2S VPN as the fallback, automatic failover is typically under 90s for route convergence in our lab, but practical failover for requests depends on client-side retries and DNS TTLs. For tighter RTOs (<30s) we suggest adding an active healthcheck-based routing appliance on your edge that moves traffic to the VPN if probe fails.

SLA: Redwood can provide a dedicated capacity SLA for the private data plane (SLO on median P95 latency and availability). PrivateLink itself is an AWS construct; our SLA bundles the end-to-end path including the endpoint and our serving fleet under a single committed latency/availability target when you purchase Dedicated capacity. I'll attach the short SLA snippet to the pilot doc.

Attachments in the drive include the cost sheet (breakdown of endpoint/packet egress vs dedicated pool commit).

Technical notes (short):
- Routing: Avoid transitive routing via peering — it creates complexity. If you need central egress for multiple BrightHarbor VPCs, use AWS Transit Gateway with interface endpoints or a central proxy stack.
- Security: Mutual TLS on top of PrivateLink; token auth enforced at the ENI. For S2S VPN we recommend IPsec with IKEv2 and BGP MD5 on the session.
- Observability: We'll publish a per-endpoint flow log and token-level latency in the Redwood Console; you can subscribe to the webhook or pull via the API.

I'll be at the pilot planning call if you'd like me to present the throughput numbers and runbooks.

— Ben
Sr Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

This reads well. A couple operational asks from procurement and security: 

- Procurement needs a short template for pricing cadence (monthly committed vs overage) so we can slot it into our cloud expense forecasts. Can you provide the commitment tiers and overage rates for Dedicated pools?
- Security wants an expected set of logs we can ingest (flow logs, TLS cert chain, request IDs). Do you have a sample log schema?
- For the canary: prefer single-AZ canary in our staging VPC, then stagger to prod AZs over 48 hours. Can you confirm you can do canary sampling at ~5% of traffic and that the canary will have identical tokenization and model configuration?

If all that checks out we can route the procurement approval this week.

Canary plan (high level):
1) Provision PrivateLink interface endpoint in BrightHarbor staging VPC (single AZ).
2) Deploy dedicated Redwood pool sized to 1.5x expected staging peak and enable request tracing.
3) Route 5% of staging inference traffic through the PrivateLink endpoint for 24 hours, monitor P95 latency and error rates.
4) If stable, scale to 25% across two AZs for 24 hours, then migrate prod over 48 hours.

I'll open the calendar invite for Tuesday 10:00 PT to run the pilot kickoff and include a 30-minute ops walkthrough (runbook + rollback).

Appreciate the quick turnaround on this — we'll keep the peering option as a lab-only path for now.
